svg.aria-label: Diagram: how expanding a subnet primary IPv4 range works and why the operation itself is non-disruptive, which configurations do not follow the expansion including firewall rules and GKE control plane authorized networks, which subnets cannot be expanded or are capped at slash 16, and why Google recommends expanding conservatively because each expansion permanently consumes neighbouring address space
svg.title: Expanding a subnet: safe to perform, irreversible in effect, and silent about policy
svg.text: A subnet can only grow, and growth does not carry your firewall rules with it.
Google says expand conservatively because you can always expand again. That inverts the usual instinct.
What expanding actually does
Expand by setting the prefix length to a SMALLER number: /24 becomes /23. There is no other
direction — you cannot shrink a primary range, and expansion cannot be undone.
It takes several minutes, and during expansion traffic within the subnet is not interrupted.
So the operation is safe. What is not safe is everything that referenced the old range.
What does NOT follow the expansion
FIREWALL RULES. If rules use the original range as a source or destination, you must ADD
rules to apply the same rules to the extended range. The subnet grows; the policy does not.
GKE: you must add the expanded range to the control plane authorized networks list.
New addresses therefore arrive governed by nothing you wrote for the old ones.
What cannot be expanded, or not far
Proxy-only subnets used exclusively for load balancer proxies cannot be expanded at all.
A subnet created by auto mode — or in a network that WAS auto mode — stops at /16,
because anything broader collides with the other automatically created subnets.
The mode chosen in #62 is still setting the ceiling three posts later.
Why conservative expansion beats one big one
Google: expand primary IPv4 ranges conservatively; you can always expand them again.
That reads backwards until you see what an expansion consumes. The range grows into the
addresses NEXT to it, permanently, and those cannot overlap any other subnet in the network
or any subnet in a PEERED network. Every expansion forecloses a neighbour you have not met.
#63 said size generously at creation. Both are right: space is free before, owned after.
The contrast worth holding: a SECONDARY range can be removed and replaced once no instances
use it. The primary range is the only part of a subnet that is permanent in both directions.
Consider address space in any network yours is OR WILL BE connected to before expanding. That
is the only sentence here about the future, and it is the one the irreversibility is about.
